name: Quba Mosque
label: Quba Mosque
camera_source: Commons cluster (4 photos), weak. Moved 28 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 90 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18051738: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'QUBA Mosque' (114 m across).
notes: The first mosque in Islam, with white domes and minarets.

text.description:
Quba Mosque is thought to be the first mosque in the world, first built in the 7th century during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad. Tradition says he laid its first stone when he stopped at the village of Quba' on his journey to Medina. The building you see today dates from a complete reconstruction begun in 1984 and inaugurated on 2 November 1986. It was designed by the Egyptian architect Abdel-Wahed El-Wakil in a traditional style and has four minarets and 56 domes. That gives you a lot of repeating shapes to work with: rows of small domes, tall slim towers and a pale, even-toned building.

The mosque stands in a large plot of about 13,500 square metres, so it is easiest to photograph from a little distance. Pick a moment when fewer people are in front of you. Keep the minarets upright by using the gridlines, and leave a little sky above them. A larger expansion of the mosque and its surroundings was announced in 2022, so what you see around it may change from visit to visit.

This is a working place of worship, so be discreet around people at prayer and avoid pointing your phone at worshippers.
text.geographic_location: In the Quba district of Medina, in the Hejaz region of Saudi Arabia. It was once a separate village outside the city, which Medina has since grown to include.
text.directions_text: Head to Quba Mosque in Medina. From there it is about 1 minute on foot to the mosque, heading west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the mosque in its setting. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole building will not fit, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes and minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front courtyard, facing the domes and minarets). The white domes and minarets framed from the open courtyard, with the wide-angle view taking in the whole building. From here the mosque sits in front of you with its minarets and domes in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a minaret with a vertical line so it stands straight. Put the horizon on the lower third and leave some sky above. For a second shot, zoom in on the row of domes. Step back a little rather than tilting the phone upwards, which makes the towers lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the light stonework keeps its detail. Do not use portrait mode for the building. Panorama can work if you stand still and pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to suit this view, as the sun should be behind you and light the face of the mosque. Late afternoon is a good second choice if you want softer light.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so dress modestly and check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements and any access limits.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing east of the mosque and facing west, morning sun should be behind the photographer and light the east-facing side of the building.
Late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
Photographing worshippers at prayer may be unwelcome, so visitors should be discreet.
Building work for the expansion may change what is visible around the mosque from one visit to the next.
Visitors should dress modestly at a mosque.

name: Prophet's Mosque
label: Prophet's Mosque
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/461699097: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Prophet's Mosque' (509 m across).
notes: The second holiest mosque in Islam, with its vast courtyard and umbrellas.

text.description:
The Prophet's Mosque (al-Masjid al-Nabawī) stands at the heart of Medina. It is the second mosque built by the Prophet Muhammad in the city, after Quba Mosque. It is also the second largest mosque, and the second holiest site in Islam after the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca. The first building dates from 622 and was far smaller than today's. It began as an open-air space used as a community centre, a court and a religious school. Later rulers expanded and decorated it again and again, so what you see now is the result of many centuries of building. The mosque also contains the graves of Muhammad and the first two caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar. Its best-known feature is the Green Dome, at the south-east corner. In 1909 it became the first place in the Arabian Peninsula to have electric lights.

The mosque photographs well because of its sheer scale, its minarets and the contrast of the green dome against pale stonework. It is too big to fit in one frame from close up, so choose what the picture is about: the long frontage, a single minaret, or the dome. Keep your phone straight and use the gridlines so the walls and towers don't lean. Be considerate of worshippers, and avoid pointing the camera at people who are praying.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the centre of Medina, the area around the Prophet's Mosque; no stations or tram stops are listed for this spot. Then find the phone icon on the map. From there the middle of the mosque is about 143 m to the north, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of the mosque. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of a section of it. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Green Dome and the tops of the minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The mosque is very large, so you will be seeing one part of it rather than all of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a minaret or wall edge with a vertical line so it stays upright. Leave some sky above the towers. For the Green Dome, zoom in and let the dome fill the middle of the frame rather than shrinking it among the buildings. If the ultra-wide stretches the edges, move back a little if you can, or use the default lens (1x) and take two shots of different parts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid, like a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is soft and the surroundings are quieter, or after sunset when the mosque is lit. Prayer times are busiest, so expect more people then.

text.access_note: This is a major place of worship and pilgrimage, and rules about who may enter, what to wear and where photography is allowed can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Islamic University of Madinah
label: Islamic University
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Islamic University Gate' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Large campus west of the city.

text.description: The Islamic University of Madinah is a public Islamic university in Medina, founded by royal decree in 1961. It began with Islamic studies and now also teaches Arabic, law, business, computing, engineering and the sciences. For a visitor with a phone, the best-looking part of it is the main entrance: a monumental gateway that faces the city, so the approach from the city side gives a clean, straight-on view. The gate photographs well because it is big, symmetrical and easy to read, and you can take it from the public side without going into the campus. Stand back far enough to fit the whole portal in, and keep the frame level so the sides of the gateway don't lean. For a quieter, more open angle, Islamic University Square shows the campus frontage and the valley setting. Keep to the public perimeter: administrative areas, classrooms and student residences need university permits. Photography is generally fine in public areas, but be discreet and ask before photographing anywhere sensitive. Avoid pointing your phone at students or staff without asking.
text.geographic_location: In the Medina area of Saudi Arabia.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so travel from central Medina to the Islamic University's main gate. Ask for the main gate on the city side. Once there, walk along the public frontage rather than into the campus. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the gateway. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and cannot fit the whole portal in. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for tighter framing of the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The campus lies to the east, beyond the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the gateway up with the middle of the frame. Keep the phone upright and level so the sides of the portal stay straight. Leave some road or forecourt in the foreground to give a sense of approach. For a quieter, more open alternative, try Islamic University Square, which shows the campus frontage and the valley setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the gate keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case vehicles or people pass through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the gateway than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: The gate and public frontage can be photographed from outside, but administrative areas, classrooms and student residences need university permits, so check the university's official site before you go.

name: Al-Baqi Cemetery
label: Al-Baqi Cemetery
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/65541621: large area 'Maqbara Al Baqeea' (716 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic cemetery beside the Prophet's Mosque.

text.description:
Al-Baqi Cemetery, also called Jannat al-Baqi, is the oldest Islamic cemetery in Medina. It is traditionally said to have been founded by the Prophet Muhammad, and many of his relatives and companions are buried here. It is a very large site, roughly 700 metres across, and the area was extended in early Islamic times to take in a neighbouring Jewish graveyard. Please come as a respectful visitor rather than a sightseer. This is a working burial ground and a place of deep feeling for Muslims.

The history shapes what you will see. Domes and mosques once stood over the graves, but they were pulled down in 1806 and again in 1926. Do not expect grand monuments. Think of calm, uncluttered pictures of the setting, not close-ups of graves.

For a phone photo, keep your distance and stay discreet. Use the default lens (1x) for the wider scene and the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the ground texture or the sky above the site. Avoid photographing worshippers, mourners or other visitors, and follow any signs or instructions from staff. Rules on photography here can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Medina, in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia. It covers a large area of the city, roughly 700 metres across.
text.directions_text: Head to Al-Baqi Cemetery (Jannat al-Baqi) in central Medina and get out. From there the cemetery's marked centre is 59 m to the north, about 1 minute on foot. Public access to the inside may be restricted, so follow any signs and check the official site before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wider setting. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details from a respectful distance. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are outside the boundary and want to include the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Bab Jibril (outside the boundary wall, near the Masjid an-Nabawi gate). The outer boundary wall of the cemetery, with the Prophet's Mosque close by, viewed from outside the grounds. Face north and keep to the public side of any boundary. Do not step into areas that are closed or marked as restricted.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. Look for simple compositions such as open ground and a wide sky, rather than anything that centres on individual graves. Leave people out of the frame, or keep them too small and distant to identify.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the main subject, then drag the exposure slider down a little. Bright sun on pale ground can wash out the detail. Turn off flash and any shutter sounds you can silence, so you do not disturb others.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually gives softer light and a calmer atmosphere. Avoid the hours around prayer times, when the area may be busier and more sensitive.

text.access_note: This is a sacred burial ground, so expect restrictions on entry and on photography, and dress modestly. Check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Entry to the cemetery and photography inside it may be restricted or controlled, and visitors are asked to dress modestly.
Early morning light is usually softer and the area is calmer than at midday.
The area may be busier around prayer times.

name: King Fahd Glorious Quran Printing Complex
label: Quran Printing Complex
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'King Fahd Glorious Quran Printing Complex' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/358191162: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'King Fahd Glorious Quran Printing Complex' (355 m across).
notes: The world's largest Quran printing facility.

text.description:
The King Fahd Glorious Quran Printing Complex is a large printing works in Medina that produces the Quran in Arabic and in many other languages. It opened in 1985 and now turns out about 10 million copies a year, with around 1,700 people working there. It has published 55 translations in 39 languages, so the scale is much of the appeal. This is a big site, more than 300 metres across, and it reads best as a wide architectural subject rather than a single detail.

From the public approach outside, you are photographing the exterior of the building. The main job is to fit its size and shape into the frame without tilting your phone upwards, which makes the walls lean inwards. Stand back far enough to keep the sides straight, switch on the gridlines, and line the grid up with the building's main horizontal edges. Then take a second shot closer in, filling the frame with a repeating pattern, a doorway or a decorative detail.

Photographs of the exterior are generally allowed, but the rules inside the complex are less clear and visits may be restricted, so respect any signs and any staff who ask you not to photograph. Dress modestly. Keep your shots to the outside unless you have been given permission, and check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The complex is on Tabuk Branch Road (also called Tabuk Road) in Medina, Saudi Arabia.
text.directions_text: The complex is on Tabuk Branch Road (Tabuk Road) in Medina. No stations or tram stops are listed nearby. Frame the exterior from the public approach outside and choose your own angle. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and cannot step back, and keep the phone level to limit distortion. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Frame the exterior from the public approach outside the King Fahd Glorious Quran Printing Complex and choose your own angle. The photo shows the complex's exterior architecture from outside. No single exterior spot is recommended. If you can arrange a visit, the visitors' gallery inside gives a looking-down view of the printing floor and its presses, but check the photography rules first.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's horizontal edges with them so the walls stay straight. Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then a closer one of a pattern, entrance or decorative detail. Keep people and vehicles at the edges of the frame if you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Do not use Live Photos or flash near the entrance or on any visit inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there is less glare on the walls.

text.access_note: Visits are restricted and may need an appointment, and photography rules differ between the outside and the inside, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mosque of Al-Ghamama
label: Al-Ghamama Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Masjid Al-Ghamamah' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Masjid Al-Sab'a' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/369055309: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Masjid Ghamama' (44 m across).
notes: White-domed mosque near the Prophet's Mosque.

text.description:
Mosque of Al-Ghamama (Masjid Al-Ghamamah) is one of the oldest mosques in Medina, and it still looks much as it did in the nineteenth century. It is traditionally linked with the place where the Prophet Muhammad led an Eid prayer in 631. The name means "cloud", after the rain clouds said to have gathered when he prayed here for rain. The first mosque was built between about 704 and 712 CE. It was renovated several times, including in 1340, 1622 and 1859, and later under the Saudi government. The building is a rectangular block. A long entrance section with five domes on its front leads to a prayer room with six domes, the largest above the mihrab.

It photographs well from outside. The white domes, rows of arches and pale stonework stand out against the sky, with an open plaza and trees in front to give the picture depth. Keep your pictures to the exterior and the plaza, because photography inside is discouraged. The mosque is in daily use for the five prayers, so wait for a clear moment, keep out of people's way and avoid pointing the phone at worshippers. A minaret at the north-west corner has a balcony with a view over the plaza. Check on the day whether visitors can go up, and otherwise just enjoy the plaza view from the ground. Gentle morning light after sunrise flatters the stone, and the arches and domes are lit at night.
text.geographic_location: In central Medina, west of Al-Masjid an-Nabawi (the Prophet's Mosque), close to its As-Salam door. It sits on its own plaza with trees in front.
text.directions_text: Check local transport options for reaching Al-Masjid an-Nabawi. The mosque is about 500 m west of the As-Salam door, so check the location on the map as you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole front and the plaza. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and arches. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough, and keep the mosque away from the edges of the frame, where it stretches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (exterior, from the surrounding plaza; the minaret at the northwest corner gives a balcony view over the plaza). The white domes, arches and stonework of the mosque's exterior, with the open plaza and trees in front. Walk on to the plaza in front of Masjid Al-Ghamamah and take your photos there. From the plaza you see the white domes, arches and stonework of the exterior, with the open plaza and trees in front. If you go up the north-west minaret (check whether this is allowed), the balcony looks down over the plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the row of domes up with a horizontal grid line, keeping the phone level so the walls do not lean. Include a patch of plaza and a tree or two in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Then take a closer shot of the arches and domes with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the domes keep their detail against the bright sky. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep the lit arches sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, just after sunrise, when the light is soft. The arches and domes are also lit up at night.

text.access_note: This is a working mosque with five daily prayers, so dress modestly, keep to the exterior and plaza, and follow any signage and notices at the mosque.

name: Miqat Dhu al-Hulayfah
label: Abyar Ali Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ميقات ذو الحليفة' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'ميقات ذي الحليفة' (way/457470976): middle (368 m across); moved 25 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/456361104: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Masjid ash-Shajarah' (115 m across).
notes: Large mosque that serves as the pilgrims' miqat.

text.description:
Miqat Dhu al-Hulayfah, also called the Mosque of the Tree, sits in Abyar Ali on the south-western side of Medina. It is a miqat, the place where pilgrims heading for Umrah or Hajj enter the state of ihram, so you will often see people in plain white garments here. The first mosque on the site was built under Umar II ibn Abdulaziz, the Umayyad governor of Medina, in the early 700s CE. It has been renovated several times since, most recently under King Fahd, who greatly enlarged it. The present building has two sets of arched galleries either side of a wide yard, with a domed spring house at the centre. There are 13 domes on the roof and five minarets around the enclosure. One minaret stands apart from the rest: square at the base, round at the top and set at a diagonal, rising to 64 metres.

That minaret is the feature that makes the photo. From the front forecourt, the arched galleries and domed roofline make a calm, repeating pattern, with the tall minaret rising above them. Keep the phone upright so the tower stands straight and leave some sky above it. Then walk into the central yard for a second, symmetrical view of the spring dome and the galleries around it. The forecourt and yard get crowded, especially during Umrah periods, so be patient and keep to the edges. Avoid flash, and do not photograph worshippers up close, especially inside the prayer halls.
text.geographic_location: In Abyar Ali, on the south-western side of Medina, several kilometres from the Prophet's Mosque. The mosque stands in its own large square enclosure with trees and pathways.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops serve this spot, so check local transport options for reaching Abyar Ali on the south-western side of Medina and ask for Miqat Dhu al-Hulayfah. The mosque building is south-east of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the mosque. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the central yard to fit in the galleries and the spring dome. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the top of the diagonal minaret and the domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front forecourt, facing the main facade and the tall minaret). The mosque's arched galleries and domed roofline with the tall, diagonally shaped minaret rising above the enclosure. From here your photo shows the arched galleries and domed roofline, with the tall, diagonally shaped minaret rising above the enclosure.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. Include some forecourt in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a second photo, go into the open central yard and shoot across it to the domed spring house and the surrounding arched galleries for a symmetrical courtyard view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stone or the minaret to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and white walls keep their detail. Do not use flash. Skip portrait mode and Live Photos of people, and do not point the phone at worshippers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time outside the busiest pilgrim periods if you can, as the forecourt and yard fill up during Umrah periods. Early morning or late afternoon is likely to give softer light on the facade.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship and pilgrim site, so dress modestly and respectfully, and check the official site before you go for current access and photography guidance.

name: Green Dome
label: Green Dome
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al-Masjid an-Nabawi' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Masjid Al-Sab'a' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/232440740: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Green Dome' (23 m across).
notes: The famous green dome over the Prophet's tomb.

text.description:
The Green Dome sits over the chamber that holds the tombs of the Prophet Muhammad and the first two caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar. It stands in the south-east corner of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina. The graves themselves cannot be seen, so the photograph is all about the dome and its setting. The colour is the draw: a soft green against the white roofline and pale sky, with two minarets either side to frame it.

The first wooden cupola on the site dates from 1279/1280. The current dome was added in 1818 under the Ottoman Sultan Mahmud II, and it was first painted green in 1837, which is how it got its name.

The best close-up view is from the western courtyard near the Bab as-Salam entrance. From there the dome appears framed between two minarets, rising above the white roofline of the mosque. A second angle is looking south over the prayer halls, with the umbrellas in the foreground. Take the photo from the courtyard and keep the dome in the upper half of the frame, with the minarets as vertical lines either side.

Be discreet. Guides advise against tripods, flash, drones and photographing people at prayer, and rules can change, so check on arrival.
text.geographic_location: In the south-east corner of the Prophet's Mosque (Al-Masjid an-Nabawi) in central Medina. The close-up viewing courtyard is on the mosque's western side, by the Bab as-Salam entrance.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stops are listed for this spot; head for the Prophet's Mosque and ask for the Bab as-Salam entrance on the western side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the dome between the two minarets. If the crowds or distance keep you back, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the dome closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is useful for the courtyard and roofline, but it makes the dome look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Al-Masjid an-Nabawi (western courtyard, near the Bab as-Salam entrance). The dome framed between two minarets, rising above the mosque's white roofline. For the close-up view, go to the western courtyard of Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, near the Bab as-Salam entrance. The view shows the dome framed between two minarets, rising above the mosque's white roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the two minarets up with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Put the dome in the upper-middle of the frame with the white roofline below it. For a second option, try the angle looking south over the prayer halls, with the umbrellas in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the green keeps its colour and the white roofline does not wash out. Turn the flash off. Skip portrait mode and Live Photos; a plain, steady shot works best here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds build up. One guide suggests the period around Fajr, when the light is soft and fewer people are about.

text.access_note: This is a place of worship, and access to some areas may be limited, so check the official site before you go and on arrival.

name: Masjid al-Qiblatayn
label: Masjid al-Qiblatayn
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'مسجد القبلتين' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/66510098: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mosque Al-Qiblatayn - Mosque of the Two Qiblas' (99 m across).
notes: The mosque of the two qiblas.

text.description:
Masjid al-Qiblatayn, the Mosque of the Two Directions, is one of the oldest mosques in Medina. It is traditionally dated to 2 AH (623 CE) and is built around the story that the Prophet Muhammad was told here to change the direction of prayer from Jerusalem to Mecca. The mosque was completely rebuilt in 1987 in a modern design, with twin domes and twin minarets, so what you photograph today is a clean, symmetrical building rather than an ancient one. The original mihrab facing Jerusalem was removed, and a small marker mihrab beneath a second, false dome recalls the earlier direction.

It photographs well because the symmetry is easy to use: two minarets, two domes and a raised courtyard that gives you room to step back. The entrance is reached from that courtyard by stairs and ramps. The wide, open space lets you fit the front of the mosque into one frame without being right up against the walls.

A travel guide describes the spacious front courtyard as a pleasant place to stroll and take photos, and it is free to walk in. Take a few frames of the whole facade first, then move closer for details such as the arches and domes. Photograph outside prayer times, never during prayers, and ask permission before photographing worshippers. A second viewpoint is across the road junction on Khalid ibn al-Walid Road, which shows the whole exterior and minarets with the street in front.
text.geographic_location: Masjid al-Qiblatayn is in the north-west of Medina, on Khalid ibn al-Walid Road, roughly 5 km north-west of the Prophet's Mosque.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, train or tram stop for this spot, so start from the Prophet's Mosque area in central Medina. The mosque is about 5 km to the north-west, best reached by taxi or hired scooter. Ask the driver for Masjid al-Qiblatayn (مسجد القبلتين), then walk up the stairs or ramps into the front courtyard. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyard to fit both minarets and the whole facade in. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the entrance. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes and minaret tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back into the raised courtyard to the north, where the entrance is, to frame the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the entrance up with the middle of the frame, so the twin minarets and domes sit evenly on either side. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. For a different view, cross to the road junction on Khalid ibn al-Walid Road and photograph the whole exterior with the street in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the walls keep their detail. Use telephoto only if you can hold the phone steady against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the walls, and the courtyard is often calmer then. Avoid prayer times, when the mosque is busy and photography is discouraged.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and respect prayer times; check the official site before you go for current access.

name: Al-Ijabah Mosque
label: Al-Ijabah Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'مسجد الإجابة' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q12242695: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Small historic mosque east of the centre.

text.description:
Al-Ijabah Mosque is a small mosque in Medina, also known as Bani Muawiyah Mosque or Al-Mubahalah Mosque. It was built in the time of the Prophet Muhammad, on land owned by Muawiyah bin Malik bin 'Auf of the tribe of As-Sus. It is best known for a hadith in Sahih Muslim, which describes the Prophet stopping here to pray for two rakats and then speaking about three wishes he made to God. The mosque stands on As-Sittin Street, in what is now the Bani Muawiyah District. It lies 580 metres from the Prophet's Mosque.

For a phone photo, the best view is the plain one: the front of the building, with the single dome and the minaret together in one frame. The dome is a simple shape against the sky, so a straight-on shot from the street works well. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines, so the minaret stays upright and does not lean. If a car or a passer-by crosses the frame, wait a moment and take the shot again. As this is a mosque, keep a respectful distance from anyone who may be praying and do not photograph people at close range without asking. Please also check the current state of the building before you go, as there may be building work and limited access.
text.geographic_location: In the Bani Muawiyah District of Medina, on As-Sittin Street, a short way north of Al-Baqi Cemetery (about 385 m) and about 580 m from the Prophet's Mosque.
text.directions_text: Start from the Prophet's Mosque area in central Medina, the nearest known landmark. The mosque is about 580 m from the Prophet's Mosque, on As-Sittin Street. Check the exact position on the map on the day before you set off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the front of the mosque with the dome and minaret. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is narrow and you cannot step back far enough, and keep the building in the middle of the frame to limit stretching.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the mosque is right in front of you, a small single-dome building with its minaret, seen from street level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical line. Keep the dome and minaret both in the frame, with some sky above them. The dome stands out against the low buildings around it, so a straight-on view shows this well. For a closer detail of the dome or minaret top, use the telephoto (2x-5x) rather than walking up to the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building does not turn into a dark shape and the sky keeps some colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the street is quiet and the light is not harsh, and avoid the busy periods around prayer times.

text.access_note: This is a mosque, so dress modestly and respectfully, and check local information before you go, as its current state may involve building work and limited access.

name: Seven Mosques
label: Seven Mosques
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'مسجد الفتح' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'مسجد الفتح' (way/1536783060): middle (12 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1544963301: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Seven Mosques' (479 m across).
notes: Group of small mosques at the Battle of the Trench site.

text.description:
The Seven Mosques is a cluster of six small historic mosques at the foot of Mount Sela (Sal') in Medina. The name says seven because some people believe there were originally seven, and because visitors often add nearby Masjid Al-Qiblatayn to their visit. The mosques are linked to the Battle of the Trench, and each is named after the person said to have been stationed there. The largest is Al-Fath, which was renovated in 1154. One of the smallest, Fatimah Az-Zahra, measures only about 4 by 3 metres, while Ali bin Abu Talib measures about 8.5 by 6.5 metres, so the sizes in the group vary a great deal.

For a phone photo, the best wide view is from the hilltop viewpoint by مسجد الفتح. This is the hilltop on the western side of the mountain, reached by a substantial flight of stairs. From up there you can take one wide shot of the whole battlefield landscape, with the complex spread out below the hill. At street level the small mosques are close together and hard to fit into one frame, so the hilltop is the easiest way to show how they sit together. Take your time on the stairs and look back as you climb, because the view opens up gradually. Photographs are fine outside the mosques but are generally restricted inside. Several of the small mosques may be closed, so frame them from outside.
text.geographic_location: In Medina, Saudi Arabia, on the southern side of Mount Sela (Sal'). The viewpoint is on the hill on the mountain's western side, with the smaller mosques of the complex lying below it.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so check the route locally before you set out for the foot of Mount Sela (Sal') in Medina. Look for the stairs up the western side of the hill to مسجد الفتح, the hilltop viewpoint for the wide shot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole landscape, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single small mosque below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (hilltop on the western side of Sal' mountain, reached by the stairs). A wide panorama of the Battle of the Trench landscape with the Seven Mosques complex visible below the hill. From there you look out over the Battle of the Trench landscape, with the Seven Mosques complex visible below the hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line so the mosques and open ground fill most of the frame. Include a little of the staircase or courtyard edge in the foreground to give a sense of height. If you want the whole sweep of the site, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mosques below to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the buildings keep their detail. Keep your phone steady against a wall or railing for panoramas.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the stairs, but there is no fixed best time. Check the sun direction on the day.

text.access_note: The hill is reached by a flight of stairs, and the Al-Fath building is closed but its courtyard and staircase are open; several of the smaller mosques may be closed, and photography is generally not allowed inside, so check current access before you go.

name: Hejaz Railway Museum
label: Hejaz Railway Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hejaz Railway Museum' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5701241: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Ottoman-era station with old steam locomotives.

text.description: The Hejaz Railway Museum sits in the grounds of Medina's restored Ottoman railway station, the last stop on the Hejaz Railway. The station building is the star here: a long, weathered stone frontage with Ottoman character that fills a phone frame well, particularly from the road side where you can step back far enough to take it all in. The museum opened in 2006 and includes a stretch of the historic track, a train shed, locomotives and other rolling stock, some of it brought from other points along the old line. Behind the entrance area you may catch glimpses of the grounds and any outdoor rolling stock, which adds a bit of depth and story to a wide shot. The museum is currently closed for refurbishment, so plan on exterior views from the road rather than a visit inside. That still makes for a worthwhile stop, because the building itself is the main subject. Keep your phone level using the gridlines so the long facade doesn't lean, and leave a little room around the edges so nothing is cut off. If traffic or railings get in the way, shift a few steps along the pavement and try again. A second viewpoint across Omar Bin Al Khattab Rd, near Masjid Anbariyah, shows the station framed by the street and the mosque's grounds. Check the current status before you set out.
text.geographic_location: In the Anbariyah area of Medina, on the grounds of the former Ottoman railway station, not far from the Prophet's Mosque.
text.directions_text: Head for the Anbariyah area of Medina, near the Prophet's Mosque, by whatever local transport suits you. Make for the Hejaz Railway Museum (the old railway station) and walk to the road in front of the facade. The phone icon on the map is right at the building, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. If you can't step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), and use the telephoto (2x or more) for stonework details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the restored Ottoman station building and its frontage, with the museum grounds and any outdoor rolling stock behind the entrance area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the roofline with a horizontal grid line so the building sits straight. Keep the whole frontage in frame, then take a closer shot of the weathered stonework. For a different view, try the alternative across Omar Bin Al Khattab Rd near Masjid Anbariyah, which frames the station with the street and the mosque's grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its texture. Use 0.5x sparingly, as it can stretch the edges of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the light is soft and traffic on the road is lighter, so you get a clean view of the facade.

text.access_note: The museum is currently closed for refurbishment, so expect exterior views from the road only; check the current status locally before you go.
